newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Rescuers search ruins after deadly Venezuela quake.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers search ruins after deadly Venezuela quake.

text.p: Rescue teams in eastern Venezuela on Thursday tried to reach survivors trapped beneath collapsed buildings by an earthquake that hit the Caribbean coast and killed at least 36 people.

Schools and office buildings were flattened by the temblor, which measured 6.9 on the open-ended Richter scale and officials said the death toll could rise from Venezuela's worst earthquake in three decades.
Many of the dead were children, crushed as schools crumbled. Another 162 people were injured and more than 500 families made homeless.
More than 16 hours after the quake, survivors were still being pulled from rubble.

"We don't know how many people are still in there but we know there are a lot because the quake hit during office hours," Jose Azocar, fire chief in the historic Caribbean city Cumana told reporters outside the remains of the six-story Seguros la Seguridad office building where at least eight died.
Eleven survivors were rescued from the building's debris, described by witnesses as "a pile of cement and metal," Azocar said.
Overall, damage was limited to a handful of buildings, witnesses said.

The majority of the deaths occurred in the small Caribbean town Cariaco about 295 miles (470 km) east of Caracas, where two schools collapsed, killing 22 people, mostly schoolchildren, Sucre State Civil Defense Director Francisco Espin told Reuters.
Another six people died in nearby Casanay, state Governor Ramon Martinez said.
At the remains of the Seguros la Seguridad tower block in Cumana firemen and medics swarmed over the mound of rubble.
Around dawn on Thursday a group clustered around one of the holes opened up in the wreckage burst into cheers and applause. Shortly afterwards a woman was carried away from the site on a stretcher.
Some of the survivors, trapped in what was the basement of the building, kept in contact with the outside world by cellular telephones, Martinez said.
Up to 70 people were thought to have been in the building at the time of the quake.
Telephone, water and electricity lines were working sporadically. Other buildings appeared to be little affected by the quake.

Details from Cariaco were more sketchy due to a number of landslides blocking the road to the town. Preliminary reports said the Raimundo Centeno Martinez high school and adjacent Valentin Valiente primary school had been flattened.
Martinez said seven children were rescued from the school ruins alive and more could still be trapped inside.
"The information which we have received is sporadic and, I would say, is not very pleasant," said Civil Defense Director Francisco Daboin.
Martinez declared the worst hit eastern Sucre state in emergency and called for urgent assistance from the government to provide lifting equipment and medical aid.
About 65 Red Cross and rescue workers left Caracas on an Air Force Hercules C130 late Wednesday with more than 14 tonnes of medical supplies and heavy equipment.

The quake, the worst to hit Venezuela since 1967, struck about 3:25 p.m. EDT (1925 GMT) Wednesday, sending panicked people into the streets in cities and towns from the capital to the furthest eastern tip of the country.
The FUNVISIS seismological institute said the first quake measured 6.9 on the open-ended Richter scale.
The epicenter was about 30 miles (49 km) off Venezuela's northeastern Caribbean coast and there were five aftershocks, the last at 5:40 p.m. EDT (2140 GMT), they said.
FUNVISIS warned that further aftershocks could occur in coming days.

Despite the size of the quake, state-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela said both production and export continued to flow smoothly. Venezuela is the largest exporter of crude oil to the United States.

Founded in 1521, Cumana is the oldest inhabited city in South America. However most of its colonial architecture was destroyed in a massive earthquake in 1797. Wednesday's earthquake was the second major tremor to strike the city of 250,000 people this century, the last in 1929.
The 1967 quake, the last to cause serious damage in Venezuela, killed 215 people in the capital and surrounding area, FUNVISIS officials said.
